question: Can activation updates of non-trainable neuron states and gradient updates of trainable biases be engineered so that their joint continuous limit reproduces Hamiltonian, Klein-Gordon, Dirac, and gauge-covariant field equations?

key_findings.claim: Author construction: for a restricted linear recurrent learning system, neuron state and trainable bias can be identified with canonical position and momentum when the loss and matrices satisfy specially chosen algebraic constraints.
key_findings.evidence: The one-neuron derivation assumes identity self-weight, linear activation, batch size one, and a single backpropagation step with dphi/dbeta=1. Matching its continuous activation/learning equations to Hamilton's equations forces a quadratic-in-beta Hamiltonian and a particular family of losses. The N-neuron version further assumes invertible B, symmetric W, and commutation WB=BW, or the linear block constraints in Eq. 2.19.

key_findings.claim: Reviewer qualification: the claimed duality is an inverse-designed formal realization, not evidence that ordinary neural-network training spontaneously produces a physical theory.
key_findings.evidence: The target Hamiltonian or field equation is specified first, after which weights, bias transforms, losses, and update rules are selected to make the algebra coincide. There is no dataset, learning task, random initialization, optimization experiment, convergence theorem, perturbation analysis, or probability that the required matrices arise under generic training. The paper itself notes the relation is many-to-one.

anchors.section: Introduction, distinction from supervised equation learning

key_findings.claim: Author construction: two different lattice update factorizations reproduce a discrete Klein-Gordon equation in the continuum limit.
key_findings.evidence: A scalar field is stored across lattice-indexed neurons. In the first realization, identity W/B activation integrates beta while the gradient of a spatial finite-difference loss updates beta. In a second, spatial finite differences move into the activation weights and a quadratic loss makes beta(t+1)=-phi(t). Both eliminate beta to yield the Klein-Gordon stencil with different temporal centering.

anchors.section: Section 3, continuum and lattice Klein-Gordon system

key_findings.claim: Author construction: antisymmetric neuron-type factors satisfying a Clifford-like algebra combine real state/trainable fields into a complex spinor obeying the continuum Dirac equation.
key_findings.evidence: The model introduces multiple neuron types and lattice-indexed tensors. One-dimensional two-type and three-dimensional four-type examples choose antisymmetric X matrices, paired forward/backward spatial differences, and a mass coupling. Four real phi and pi components are assembled into a four-component complex psi; Kronecker products then satisfy gamma-matrix anticommutation and give Eq. 4.37.

key_findings.claim: Reviewer physics audit: deriving the pointwise continuum Dirac equation does not establish a consistent lattice fermion field theory.
key_findings.evidence: The manuscript does not analyze the lattice spectrum, fermion doubling, chiral symmetry, unitarity, canonical anticommutation, path-integral measure, anomalies, or continuum renormalization. Standard naive finite-difference Dirac operators generically contain spurious species. The manuscript's paired one-sided differences may alter that issue, but no pole or dispersion calculation is supplied, so physical equivalence beyond the formal continuum stencil is unverified.

key_findings.claim: Gauge covariance is obtained by inserting a background connection into dynamic weights and biases, not by deriving gauge-field dynamics from learning.
key_findings.evidence: A global discrete U(1) rotation is promoted to a position/time-dependent rotation. Extra A terms are then added so the finite differences transform covariantly, under an approximation equating derivatives at nearby lattice points. The final paragraph explicitly says A_mu is a background gauge field whose equations must be introduced independently, perhaps at the learning level.

key_findings.claim: The paper supplies no empirical or numerical evaluation, so stability and robustness of the discrete updates remain unknown.
key_findings.evidence: All results are symbolic manipulations of linear update equations. There are no simulated trajectories, convergence orders, conservation-error measurements, lattice-spacing sweeps, learned parameter recovery, perturbations away from exact matrix identities, or comparisons with conventional integrators or physics-informed neural models.

method.core_idea: Identify recurrent activation dynamics with a canonical coordinate update and gradient-based bias learning with the conjugate-momentum update, then choose tensor stencils and losses that factor known lattice field equations into those two steps.
method.mechanism: Take a continuous-time limit of linear activation plus one-step backpropagation; solve algebraic conditions on W, B, A, V, and the loss for Hamiltonian form; place neurons on a spatial lattice; encode scalar Laplacians with symmetric weights and spinor derivatives with antisymmetric neuron-type matrices; finally add connection terms to weights/biases so local U(1) rotations are covariant.
assumptions: Linear activation and learning dynamics are an adequate description; intrinsically nonlinear learning is explicitly outside the derivation.
Mini-batch size is one and only a single backpropagation step contributes, giving the assumed local derivative dphi/dbeta.
The unit-step discrete recurrence admits the stated continuous-time interpretation.
Bias transform B is invertible and required weight/bias matrices are symmetric, commuting, or satisfy exact Clifford-like identities.
Loss functions may be engineered for algebraic correspondence even when they are not standard bounded-below statistical objectives.
Spatial fields and derivatives are smooth enough for the approximate local-gauge finite differences.
Classical lattice equations are the target; quantum statistics, gravity, and interacting gauge dynamics are absent.

techniques.role: Map non-trainable state and trainable bias to canonical coordinate and momentum.
Solve for a loss whose gradient update reproduces a chosen Hamiltonian equation.
Split second-order Klein-Gordon dynamics into activation and learning recurrences.
Implement Clifford/gamma structure needed for a Dirac-like first-order equation.
Insert U(1) background gauge connections into weight and bias tensors.

evaluations.setting: Single- and N-neuron linear continuous-time limits
evaluations.metric: Exact symbolic equality with canonical Hamilton equations
evaluations.result: Equality holds for specially constructed losses and symmetry/invertibility/commutation constraints.
evaluations.baseline: Direct Hamilton equations; no numerical baseline.

evaluations.setting: Scalar neurons on a three-dimensional unit lattice
evaluations.result: Two activation/learning factorizations yield temporally shifted discrete Klein-Gordon stencils.

evaluations.setting: Two neuron types in 1D and four neuron types in 3D
evaluations.metric: Continuum-limit gamma-matrix anticommutation and equation matching
evaluations.result: Selected antisymmetric matrices assemble state and trainable variables into a complex spinor satisfying a formal Dirac equation.
evaluations.baseline: Continuum free Dirac equation; no lattice-spectrum validation.

evaluations.setting: Local U(1) rotations on the discrete Dirac construction
evaluations.metric: Approximate covariance of the update equations
evaluations.result: Added dynamic weight/bias components transform as temporal/spatial gauge connections and give the minimally coupled continuum equation.
evaluations.baseline: Prescribed background Abelian gauge field; its own dynamics are not modeled.

limitations: Author-acknowledged: the analysis is classical and excludes quantum and gravitational effects.
Author-acknowledged: intrinsically nonlinear learning phenomena are not captured by the linear Hamiltonian description.
Author-acknowledged: the field-theory/learning relation is many-to-one rather than an invertible map.
Author-acknowledged: gauge-field dynamics must be introduced independently; only a background connection is represented.
Reviewer-identified: no actual network is trained, so 'emergence' is not demonstrated under data-driven learning or generic initialization.
Reviewer-identified: exact matrix symmetries and hand-built losses encode the desired physics in advance.
Reviewer-identified: the continuum step and one-step derivative assumption omit finite-step backpropagation and optimizer-state effects.
Reviewer-identified: some constructed objectives are indefinite or need not be bounded below, weakening their interpretation as trainable losses.
Reviewer-identified: no stability, consistency-order, conservation, or perturbation analysis is provided.
Reviewer-identified: the Dirac lattice construction does not address doubling, chirality, anomalies, or fermionic quantization.
Reviewer-identified: only U(1) background coupling is treated; non-Abelian fields, gauge action, and Gauss constraints are absent.
failure_modes: Small violations of symmetry or commutation constraints can destroy the canonical correspondence.
Gradient descent on an indefinite constructed loss can diverge even if its formal update matches a target equation locally.
Unit-step recurrences can be numerically unstable for masses or spatial frequencies outside the finite-difference stability region.
Naive lattice Dirac modes can include unphysical fermion doublers or wrong anomaly structure.
A dynamic parameter called a gauge field may not obey Maxwell/Yang-Mills equations, constraints, or energy conservation.
The continuous-time limit can hide discretization artifacts and off-by-one temporal staggering.
Generic nonlinear activations, minibatches, multi-step backpropagation, momentum, and Adam break the derived identities.
reusable_insights: Coupled forward-state and parameter-update dynamics can be analyzed as one enlarged dynamical system rather than separate inference and training phases.
A second-order field equation admits multiple factorizations into alternating state and parameter updates; the factorization choice determines numerical properties.
Symmetric versus antisymmetric parameter blocks provide a compact design language for scalar versus spinor-like channels.
Formal equation matching should be separated from emergence: test attraction basins, perturbation robustness, and learnability before making an ontological claim.
For lattice claims, validate dispersion, species count, conserved currents, gauge constraints, and continuum convergence—not only pointwise algebra.
open_questions: Do the proposed recurrences have stable finite-step regimes and the expected numerical convergence order?
Can ordinary optimization from random initialization learn the required tensor symmetries without hard-coding them?
What is the spectrum of the discrete Dirac update, and does it contain fermion doublers or nonunitary modes?
Can a bounded-below loss and a standard optimizer realize the same Hamiltonian correspondence?
How should gauge-field kinetic dynamics, Gauss-law constraints, and non-Abelian transformations appear in learning variables?
Which nonlinear Hamiltonian or dissipative systems can be represented when the linear-order restriction is removed?
Can the correspondence yield a measurable algorithmic advantage over symplectic integrators or Hamiltonian neural networks?

competitive_landscape.title: Hamiltonian Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Greydanus et al. learn an unknown Hamiltonian from trajectory data and empirically test conservation and prediction. Vanchurin instead hand-constructs activation/parameter updates whose algebra equals a known Hamiltonian system; it is a representation duality without learning or predictive evaluation.

competitive_landscape.title: Neural Ordinary Differential Equations
competitive_landscape.difference: Chen et al. make a neural vector field a differentiable ODE component and train it end to end with adaptive solvers. The reviewed paper takes a continuous limit of recurrent activation plus parameter learning itself and seeks equation identity, but provides no solver, adjoint, or experiment.

competitive_landscape.title: A duality connecting neural network and cosmological dynamics
competitive_landscape.difference: Krippendorf and Spannowsky already match continuous gradient-descent network dynamics to scalar-field cosmology and empirically test effective parameters. Vanchurin uses activation and trainable variables as canonical pairs and extends formal constructions to Klein-Gordon, Dirac, and background U(1) fields, but omits empirical tests.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning Neural Hamiltonian Dynamics: A Methodological Overview
competitive_landscape.difference: Chen et al. synthesize data-driven Hamiltonian architectures, symplectic integration, generalized inputs, and limitations such as conservation assumptions and compute. That mature literature provides the learnability and numerical-validation context missing from the reviewed formal duality.

competitive_landscape.title: Naive Lattice Fermion without Doublers
competitive_landscape.difference: Guo et al. directly analyze poles of a forward-difference lattice Dirac operator and explain which hermiticity assumption is traded to evade doubling. Vanchurin matches a continuum Dirac stencil but does not calculate its lattice spectrum or state which no-go assumption its asymmetric differences relax.

competitive_landscape.title: Resolving the spurious-state problem in the Dirac equation with finite difference method
competitive_landscape.difference: Zhang et al. explicitly diagnose spurious finite-difference Dirac states and alternate forward/backward derivatives while preserving a Hermitian Hamiltonian. This is close to Vanchurin's asymmetric stencil and illustrates the spectral validation required before treating it as a physical fermion theory.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Hamiltonian position/momentum dynamics are dual to neural activation/learning dynamics, allowing scalar, spinor, and gauge fields to emerge from symmetric, antisymmetric, and dynamic neural parameters.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper gives explicit algebraic matrix/loss constructions for canonical dynamics, two Klein-Gordon factorizations, Clifford-structured Dirac updates, and U(1)-covariant background connections.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: Using trainable variables themselves as conjugate dynamical fields and organizing scalar/spinor/gauge cases through parameter-tensor symmetry is an unusual formal construction. But continuous-depth, Hamiltonian-learning, neural/physical duality, and lattice-field correspondences all predate it. Because the desired equations are encoded in advance and neither training emergence nor lattice consistency is tested, the contribution is best viewed as a formal representation recipe, not evidence that field theories emerge generically from neural learning.

reviewer_notes: All 17 extracted pages were reviewed. Competing primary sources were checked on official NeurIPS, arXiv, and APS publisher pages on 2026-08-23. The audit distinguishes formal continuum equation matching from data-driven emergence and flags untested lattice-fermion consistency.
